note: Fool's Mate: pushing the f-pawn and the g-pawn opens the diagonal to White's king, and Black's queen gives checkmate on h4 as early as move two.
Moving the f-pawn early opens the diagonal to the king. A queen check on the h-file can then be checkmate or win the rook in the corner.

moves: Bg4 Nxe5 Bxd1 Bxf7+ Ke7 Nd5#
note: Légal's Mate: the knight moves out of the pin and leaves the queen to be taken. If the queen is taken, the bishop checks on f7 and the knights give checkmate.
Giving up a bishop for the pawn on f7 or f2 just to stop the king castling rarely works: the king steps away to safety and the attacker is left a piece down for a pawn.
Scholar's Mate: White's queen and bishop both attack the pawn on f7, and if Black develops without defending it the queen takes it with checkmate. Black stops it with a pawn to g6 or the queen to e7.
Scholar's Mate: White's queen and bishop both attack the pawn on f7, and if Black develops without defending it the queen takes it with checkmate. Black stops it with a pawn to g6 or the queen to e7.

Damiano Defense: defending e5 with the f-pawn weakens the king. White's knight can take on e5 anyway, because recapturing lets the queen check on h5, take the e5 pawn with check and go on to win the rook.

moves: Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 Qb3 b5 Nxb5 cxb5 Bxb5+
note: As in Morphy's Opera Game, Black's early bishop pin costs time: White gets the bishop pair and a lead in development, then sacrifices a piece to open lines against the king still in the centre.
In the Two Knights Defense White's knight on g5 attacks f7 together with the bishop. Black has to block with the pawn to d5; a quiet move lets the knight take on f7 and fork the queen and rook.

Fried Liver Attack: when Black recaptures on d5 with the knight, White sacrifices a knight on f7 to drag the king into the centre, then attacks the pinned knight on d5 with queen and bishop. Moving the knight to a5 instead avoids it.

moves: Nd4 Nxe5 Qg5 Nxf7 Qxg2 Nxd4
note: Blackburne Shilling Gambit: Black's knight on d4 invites White to take the e5 pawn. Then the queen comes to g5, attacking the knight and the g2 pawn together, and White's kingside collapses. White should simply take the knight on d4.
Noah's Ark Trap: when White's queen recaptures on d4, Black's pawns advance with gain of time. The c-pawn attacks the queen and then moves on to c4, shutting in the bishop on b3, which is lost.
After the exchange on c6 White cannot win the e5 pawn at once: when the knight takes it, Black's queen comes to d4 and forks the knight and the e4 pawn, winning the pawn back.
Fishing Pole Trap: Black leaves a knight on g4 to be taken by the h-pawn. Taking it opens the h-file for Black's rook and queen, and the attack on the castled king usually ends in checkmate.
Mortimer Trap: the e5 pawn looks free, but once Black's c-pawn has attacked the bishop the queen checks on a5 and picks up the knight on e5.

In the Petrov, after White's knight takes on e5 Black must first drive it away with the d-pawn before taking on e4. Taking on e4 at once lets White's queen pin the knight on the e-file, and moving the knight away then loses the queen to a discovered check.

moves: Bg5 Nxe4 Bxd8 Bxf2+ Ke2 Bg4#
note: Stafford Gambit: Black gives up a pawn for fast development and traps. The best known: White pins the knight with the bishop, the knight takes on e4 anyway, and if White takes the queen the bishop checks on f2 and the other bishop gives checkmate.
Vienna Gambit: taking the f-pawn is a mistake here, because White's e-pawn advances and attacks the knight, which has no good square and has to go back home.

Siberian Trap: with Black's queen and knight both aimed at h2, chasing the knight with the h-pawn loses at once. The other knight jumps to d4 to remove the defender of h2, and the queen mates there or White loses the queen.

In the Advance Variation the fight is over the d4 pawn, which Black attacks with queen and knights. Taking it too early with the knight loses the queen: after the exchanges a bishop check uncovers White's queen against it.
When White's queen stands on e2 behind the knight on e4, Black's e-pawn is pinned to the king. Developing the second knight then allows White's knight to give a smothered checkmate on d6.

Elephant Trap: White takes the d5 pawn believing the knight on f6 is pinned. Black takes back with the knight, gives up the queen, wins White's queen with a bishop check on b4 and ends up a piece ahead.

Cambridge Springs: Black's queen on a5 pins the knight on c3 and looks along the rank at the bishop on g5. A careless developing move lets Black's knight jump to e4, and after the exchanges on g5 and c4 a piece is lost.

moves: e3 Bb4+ Bd2 dxe3 Bxb4 exf2+ fxg1=N+
note: Lasker Trap: if White attacks the advanced d-pawn with the e-pawn, Black checks with the bishop on b4. After the natural block and capture Black's pawn takes on f2 with check and then promotes to a knight with check, winning.

moves: b5 a4 c6 axb5 cxb5 Qf3
note: In the Queen's Gambit Accepted Black should not hold on to the c4 pawn with the b-pawn. White undermines the pawns with a4, and after the exchanges the queen attacks the rook along the long diagonal and wins material.

moves: Qb4+ Bd2 Qxb2 Bc3 Bb4 Qc1#
note: Englund Gambit trap: Black's queen checks on b4 and takes the b2 pawn. If White then defends with the bishop on c3, Black pins it with the bishop on b4 and wins the rook in the corner or mates on c1.
Kieninger Trap: Black's queen stands on e7 behind the knight on e5. If White takes the bishop on b4 with the a-pawn, the knight gives a smothered checkmate on d3, because White's e-pawn is pinned.
